messages.subject: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
parts:
Dear all,

I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.

The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.

Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the recent paper by Goldstein et al.

My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).

On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 9b1f1220a2b07d1e
messages.subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
parts:
Hi Marc and all--

The question "what is a site" has given me a lot of confusion in past work with occupancy models + camera traps. My preferred approach has been to define a "site" at the camera level and interpret the estimated occupancy probability as the probability that the area surveyed by the camera was used by at least one individual of the species of interest during the camera's deployment. I think of this as an "asymptotic" occupancy probability following Efford and Dawson. Discretizing space could be useful for defining the scale at which the occupancy probability is calculated, but I have the feeling that it wouldn't necessarily be meaningful for defining latent states that are shared between cameras. Then you'd end up with an asymptotic occupancy probability that I'd interpret as the probability that an animal uses at least one camera in the spatial unit at least once.

To me there are two big outstanding questions with the above, regardless of how sites are defined, which are (1) what is the spatial scale at which the "site use" of the area sampled by a camera varies (related to animal movement), and (2) does "rate of site use" actually tell us anything meaningful about biology? Per #2, there's some good recent work arguing that camera-level "occupancy" is not actually correlated with density, especially when individual animal movement rates vary (Parsons et al.; Steenweg et al.; Stauffer et al.).

A group I collaborate with has a review paper coming out any day now where we give our thoughts on some issues related to animal movement, occupancy, detection, and density. I'll link to it in this thread once it's published.

I definitely recommend wide temporal intervals for your discrete detection histories!

Best,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
parts:
Hi all,

Marc, I've been working on an occupancy model approach for passive acoustic recorders which would also work for camera traps. The likelihood is defined here and it pretty well aligns with what you said: the idea is to split the deployment period into shorter occasions within which you're willing to assume closure, then occupancy and detection is estimated for each occasion. One of the things that makes it identified is that you often get multiple detections within a period so you can use a continuous time formulation (either exponential with something like a Hawkes process to account for non-independence) or Poisson. 

Cheers,

Matt

messages.author: daaeb91800c54fd1
messages.subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
parts:
Hi Marc,

The spOccupancy package has been a game changer for us.  We've been monitoring wildlife occupancy across 40,000 km2 of the Canadian Rockies for the last twelve years with variable camera trap effort in some regions.  As you know, the spOccupancy functions can incorporate temporal and spatial autocorrelation and the resulting maps for spatial predictions of annual occupancy and changes in occupancy look much more reasonable compared to predictions that ignore spatial autocorrelation.  

Spatially imbalanced study designs can also affect the interpretation of occupancy when summarised across a study.  For that reason, I currently predict occupancy (use) for a grid of cells across the study area and summarise occupancy based on those gridded predictions rather than predictions for each camera site.

Ben raises a good point about occupancy-abundance relationships.  Interestingly, we found that declining trends for wolverine density and occupancy were highly correlated within our study area.  Barrueto et al 2022.

Jesse Whittington
Wildlife Ecologist
Banff National Park

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
parts:
Hey Marc and all,

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made. 

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

Cheers,

John

parts:
Hi all,

Marc's question about the definition of a site in camera-trap surveys motivated me to reach out for feedback about an analysis I'm conducting. It's an unusual use case for occupancy modeling, as far as I can tell.

I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level. 

I have daily reports of disease occurrence, including negative test results, per health facility (i.e., 40K sites) for the last 5 years throughout Brazil. For my analysis, I plan to summarize these reports as weekly or biweekly detections. I'm very interested in using the occupancy framework, as these diseases are commonly underdetected and not diagnosed when present. These diseases are present for large periods of time (during summer and fall), so I plan to define seasons as semesters.

Before going forward with my analyses, I would love to hear your thoughts on two particular points:

1. Do you foresee any problem with applying occupancy models to the previously described disease data? Similar to camera traps, people with the disease can go to multiple sites (i.e., attend different health facilities), so the closure assumption might not be reasonable. Marc's email made me think more about the definition of my sites and the need to interpret the occupancy estimates as occurrence. 

2. The distribution of the sites (i.e., health facilities) is not uniform. Some health facilities are very close to one another, especially in highly populated areas. If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?

Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!

Best regards,

Juliana

Hey Marc and all,

 

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made. 

 

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

 

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

 

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

 

Cheers,

 

John

Hi Juliana--

This is a very interesting application.

The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.

Best,
Ben

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.

Hi Juliana--

This is a very interesting application.

The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.

Best,
Ben

Dear Juliana,

 

this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).

 

About your two questions:

  1. I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
  2. I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.

 

Couple other comments:

  1. People are welcome to ask general questions about HMs such as occupancy models on this list, but obviously, as soon as it gets more specific about some software for which there are special, dedicated email lists, it might be better to ask there, or at least to also ask there. Jeff Doser now has an spOcc-Abu mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users. Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well
  2. To me, the most important modeling rule is “Start simple”. While SVC models may in many ways be wonderful, they are also quite complex and may be hard to fit in practice. I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
  3. What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
  4. About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out this paper, among others.

 

Good luck with your fascinating project !

 

Best regards  -- Marc

parts:
Dear colleagues,

many thanks for your many, valuable and thought-provoking messages about my question. Makes me think that perhaps the most neglected part of all the quantitative things we do is study design and that perhaps a book ought to be written about sampling design in species distribution models.

Best regards  --- Marc

From: John Clare <jcl...@wisc.edu>
Sent: Friday, November 1, 2024 18:27
To: Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>; hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?

Hey Marc and all,

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made. 

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

Cheers,

John


From: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>
Sent: Thursday, October 31, 2024 2:08 PM
To: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
 
Dear all,

I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.

The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.

Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the recent paper by Goldstein et al.

My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).

On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.

Best regards  --- Marc

parts:
Hi Marc and all,

Sorry for being late to the discussion, but just caught up to it.

I actually used occupancy models for a similar camera-trap data set. We had information on 8 species, which we analyzed as single-species, dynamic occupancy models.
It was 11 years of data, 121 camera-trap sites, imbalanced data between different species too.
Cameras were active year-round for 24/7, motion triggered. There were also missing data years, which we treated as NA. 
The focus of our analysis was seasonality, so we pooled data into months, and my primary occasions were seasons, and secondary occasions were months within seasons for repetition to calculate detection too.
Cameras were roughly in the center of 2 x 2 km2 grids, therefore, as Marc wrote in his previous e-mail, we calculated more like a "probability of use".
Since we were interested in changes in the habitat use with seasons, our focus was more on colonization and local extinction (which we called "desertion" for the same reason with "probability of use).
This work is published: https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article/105/1/122/7450311 
Code is also on GitHub: https://github.com/dilsaddt/NorthAnatolia_2022_singlesp_seasonal_habitat_use

If this could be helpful to anyone, I'm glad. 
And of course if there are any questions I'm happy to answer.
Best,
Dilsad

Hi Juliana,

just reading up some on false positive models and the Guillera-Arroita et al. (MEE, 2017) paper made me think that perhaps you might consider multi-level occupancy models. Perhaps that might be another way to dealing with spatial structure in the occurrence of the disease ? In addition, you may want to think about false positives in addition to false negatives. See also the paper by John Clare and colleagues, which extends consideration from simple occupancy to abundance and other population metrics.

Hey,

So then perhaps the number of truly infected individuals z is binomially distributed where N is the number that came in and tested and psi is the infection prevalence

z ~ Binomial(N, psi)

where the number of positive tests y is binomially distributed with detection probability p 

y ~ Binomial(z, p)

I'm not sure how well identified the detection and prevalence probabilities would be without some strong assumptions (such as the closure assumption we make in occupancy models).

I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.

Agreed. More and more I'm just thinking of occupancy as accounting for zero-inflation, and I'm thinking less about the ecological interpretation of this zero-inflation.

Hi Juliana--

This is a very interesting application.

The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?

I agree with Marc that the issue of the same infected individuals testing positive at multiple facilities sounds rare enough to be observed.

I think it will be very important to account for the variable "effort" between facilities with different testing rates. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.

Best,
Ben

Dear Juliana,

 

this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).

 

About your two questions:

  1. I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
  2. I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.

 

Couple other comments:

  1. People are welcome to ask general questions about HMs such as occupancy models on this list, but obviously, as soon as it gets more specific about some software for which there are special, dedicated email lists, it might be better to ask there, or at least to also ask there. Jeff Doser now has an spOcc-Abu mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users. Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well
  2. To me, the most important modeling rule is “Start simple”. While SVC models may in many ways be wonderful, they are also quite complex and may be hard to fit in practice. I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
  3. What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
  4. About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out this paper, among others.

 

Good luck with your fascinating project !

 

Best regards  -- Marc

If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?

 

Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!

Hi Juliana--

This is a very interesting application.

The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?

I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.

Ben

Dear Juliana,

 

this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).

 

About your two questions:

  1. I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
  2. I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.

 

Couple other comments:

  1. People are welcome to ask general questions about HMs such as occupancy models on this list, but obviously, as soon as it gets more specific about some software for which there are special, dedicated email lists, it might be better to ask there, or at least to also ask there. Jeff Doser now has an spOcc-Abu mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users. Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well
  2. To me, the most important modeling rule is “Start simple”. While SVC models may in many ways be wonderful, they are also quite complex and may be hard to fit in practice. I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
  3. What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
  4. About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out this paper, among others.

 

Good luck with your fascinating project !

 

Best regards  -- Marc

I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level.

If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?

 

Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!

 

Best regards,

On Fri, Nov 1, 2024 at 12:27 PM 'John Clare' via hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

 

Hey Marc and all,

 

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made. 

 

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

 

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

 

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

 

Cheers,

 

John
